articleTitle: The US military seems to be getting nervous about the launch supply crunch
summary: The Pentagon’s Office of Strategic Capital announced conditional loan commitments of $150 million each to Stoke Space and Rocket Lab to expand launch capacity as SpaceX moves toward retiring its Falcon rockets. The article describes growing military launch requirements, problems with United Launch Alliance’s Vulcan rocket, and Rocket Lab’s increased Neutron pricing amid constrained launch supply.

coreControversy.corporateClaim: SpaceX plans to retire Falcon if Starship is fulfilling its promise. Rocket Lab attributes Neutron’s price increase from $55 million to $70 million per launch to a surge in bookings, and Peter Beck says launch is extremely constrained.
coreControversy.criticismOrAlarm: The article suggests defense officials see Falcon retirement as a potential national security risk. Vulcan has been grounded twice in the last two years, forcing several national security missions to SpaceX, while projected military requirements have risen to up to 249 medium-to-heavy-lift launches through the early 2030s, more than double the expectation just two years ago.
coreControversy.regulatoryOrHistoricalPrecedent: Since the 1990s, military space officials have pursued assured access to space by supporting at least two US rocket programs capable of launching national security satellites. Previous support included direct subsidies, development funding, and launch contracts at premium prices to obtain technical and financial insight, schedule priority, and, in some cases, keep providers in business.

hiddenCatchesAndLimits: Both $150 million loans are conditional and subject to financial, legal, technical, investment, due diligence, and other requirements; the article does not establish completed disbursement.
SpaceX’s commercial Falcon 9 ordering cutoff concerns launches after 2028, not an immediate end to all Falcon operations.
The Space Force can place Falcon 9 and Falcon Heavy orders through 2029, with actual launches extending through 2033.
SpaceX’s planned final Falcon retirement depends on Starship fulfilling its promise; the article supplies no fixed retirement date.
Starship may eventually launch national security payloads, but SpaceX’s near-term priority is its own Starlink Internet satellites and Starmind orbital data centers.
Vulcan’s solid rocket booster problems have grounded it twice in the last two years and forced several national security missions to SpaceX.

Eligibility to compete does not establish operational readiness: among Blue Origin, Rocket Lab, Stoke Space, Relativity Space, and Impulse Space, only Blue Origin has flown a rocket that could meet the Space Force’s requirements.
Rocket Lab, Stoke Space, and Relativity Space are developing launch vehicles; Impulse Space is working on in-space propulsion.
The stated Nova debut timing applies to Nova Pathfinder, not Nova Block 2.
Nova Pathfinder’s debut is described as sometime next year, and Neutron’s first launch as next year; neither is presented as a completed milestone.
Neutron’s price increased from $55 million to $70 million per launch while the vehicle remained unproven.
Rocket Lab’s backlog of 117 launches combines Neutron and Electron orders; it is not a Neutron-only backlog.
